name: The Willem de Zwijger Oak of Prins Hendrikplein
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB), entry nr 1678392, netherlands-lrmb register
access: Free. Public square, open at all times.
transport: About 1 km north of Apeldoorn station, on foot.
verify_notes: LRMB nr 1678392, 'Zomereik Willem de Zwijgerboom', tree-level coordinate, owner_category gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=ja. Planted 24 April 1933 by Lily Roosmale Nepveu (mayor's daughter) on Prins Hendrikplein opposite the former Koninklijke HBS, to mark the 400th anniversary of William of Orange's birth (born 1533; two of the ironwork's stone posts carry the years 1533 and 1933). The young tree was grown at Berg en Bos nursery by overseer J. Verschuur and transported to the square by horse-drawn cart decorated in orange. Pieter Puype designed the surrounding wrought-iron fence, which weaves the Nassau lion and the Orange hunting horn into a repeating figure-8 motif. Second source (apeldoorndirect.nl, independent local news site) corroborates the commemorative planting and adds that the oak grew unusually fast and thick because it was planted in the enriched soil of a former rose garden on the site, reportedly now thicker than 300-year-old oaks at nearby Paleis Het Loo -- a striking anecdote worth leading with, though the girth itself is not documented in either source (girth_cm not recorded). Geheugen van Apeldoorn (municipal heritage site) carries near-identical wording to the register's own history text, likely a shared origin, so treat it as confirming rather than as a fully independent third source; apeldoorndirect.nl is the genuinely independent second source. No dated recent photo found confirming the tree today, but a landmarked, fenced commemorative oak on a public square with an active municipal heritage listing is a low-risk case for continued presence; flagged for that reason only. Note: apeldoorndirect.nl's own summary called it the '400th anniversary of his death' but the register's primary-source detail (two dated posts, 1533/1933) is clearly a birth-year commemoration; used the register's figure.
